statement: EVALI (e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury) was a surveillance case definition: vaping or dabbing in the previous 90 days, a lung infiltrate on imaging, no other plausible diagnosis, and negative infection testing (confirmed cases) or an infection judged not the sole cause (probable cases). The CDC authors say its high sensitivity likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI. By 14 January 2020 the CDC had been told of 2,668 hospitalized patients (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable): median age 24, 66% male; weekly admissions peaked in the week of 15 September 2019 and fell afterwards. Of the 2,022 patients (76%) with information on what they had vaped or dabbed in the previous 3 months, 82% reported a THC-containing product, 57% a nicotine-containing product, 41% both and 14% nicotine only; products were unknown for 24% and were not checked against what was in the devices (in the lung-fluid study, THC or its breakdown products were found in 9 of 11 patients who said they had not used THC products in the 90 days before illness). The CDC authors give three possible reasons for the nicotine-only reports: patients not reporting or not knowing what they vaped, some patients not having EVALI, or accurate reports. Deaths and intensive care are second-hand: CDC figures quoted in the laboratory papers give 52 deaths among about 2,400 reported cases by 12 December 2019 and 47% needing intensive care; the update read gives neither, nor outcomes after discharge. Vitamin E acetate, a form of vitamin E sold online as a diluent or thickener for cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients in 16 states (94%; editors' exact 95% interval 84% to 99%), including all 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction), and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, none of whom vaped THC (0% to 4%); other additives tested were found in at most one patient. FDA testing, quoted second-hand, found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products. In 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids from cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, 23 (64%) held vitamin E acetate (16% to 57% by mass) and 13 held none above 1%; 31 of the 36 held at least one pesticide (editors' count), a pattern the authors judge intermittent and not due to a single pesticide. These findings come from different laboratories, patients and sample types and point the same way, but they do not show cause: the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC, so the contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from other features of vaping THC products in 2019; no fluid from people who vaped the same products without injury was tested; none of these studies tested whether inhaling it injures the lung (the authors say laboratory studies are needed); the CDC authors state that "evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern" in some cases; and a screen of 38 cartridges listed many other chemicals by library match, without counts per cartridge. The cartridge papers call the products illicit or counterfeit; neither describes how this was established. The sources implicate certain vaping products, mostly THC-containing cartridges, and an additive in them. None tested whether THC or cannabis itself injures the lung, or looked at cannabis smoked or eaten or flower vaporized in dry-herb devices; the one screen with medical-grade cartridges (number not stated) found retinol acetate rather than vitamin E acetate in them, and fewer listed contaminants, though some harmful chemicals were identified. So the sources neither show that other forms of cannabis carry this injury nor show that they are free of it. Funding as printed: CDC authors for the surveillance report; National Cancer Institute, FDA Center for Tobacco Products and Ohio State University for the lung-fluid study; none external for the two cartridge studies; no industry funding is printed.
plain: EVALI was an outbreak of lung injury in people who vaped, mostly in 2019. By January 2020, 2,668 people in hospital had been reported to the US CDC; most were young (median age 24) and two thirds were male. Of those who said what they had vaped, most had used products with THC, and some had used only nicotine products. Vitamin E acetate, an oil sold for thickening cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, who did not vape THC. It was also found in the liquid of about two thirds of 36 cartridge samples from 10 patients in New York. This does not prove that it caused the injury: these studies did not test that, the volunteers were not people who vaped THC and stayed well, and the CDC says other chemicals are not ruled out. These studies point to certain vaping products (mostly THC cartridges, which the authors call illicit or counterfeit) and an additive in them. They did not test cannabis smoked, eaten or vaporized as plant material. One small screen of medical-grade cartridges did not find the additive in them. So the studies cannot say whether other forms of cannabis carry the same risk.
population: People hospitalized with EVALI in the US (2,668 reported to CDC by 14 January 2020); 51 of them with lung fluid tested in 16 states; 10 New York patients whose cartridges were tested (38 samples)
exposure: Vitamin E acetate found in patients' lung fluid and in vaping cartridge fluid (cartridges that held THC or other cannabinoids)
comparator: Lung fluid from 99 healthy volunteers in an unrelated study, none of whom vaped THC; no comparison cartridges within the cartridge studies
magnitude: Surveillance (CDC, 14 January 2020): 2,668 hospitalized (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable); median age 24 (13 to 85); 66% male; among 2,022 with product information: any THC 82% (1,650), any nicotine 57% (1,162), both 41% (834), THC only 33% (669), nicotine only 14% (274), neither 2% (44); peak 215 admissions in the week of 15 September 2019. Second-hand: 52 deaths among 2,409 reported cases by 12 December 2019 (about 2%, editors' calculation); 47% needed intensive care in an earlier CDC report. Lung fluid (Blount et al.): vitamin E acetate in 48 of 51 patients (94%; editors' exact 95% CI 83.8% to 98.8%) against 0 of 99 healthy volunteers (0% to 3.7%); 25 of 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction; 86.3% to 100%) and 23 of 26 probable cases; THC or metabolites 40 of 47 (85%), including 9 of 11 who reported no THC product use; nicotine or metabolites 30 of 47 (64%); coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39, all other priority substances 0 of 12 to 49. Cartridges (Duffy et al.): vitamin E acetate in 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%; exact 95% CI 46% to 79%, treating fluids as independent) at 16 to 57% by mass, from 10 patients; 13 without it, 12 of which held medium-chain triglyceride oil; 31 of 36 with at least one pesticide (editors' count); update to 12 December 2019 without methods: 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) from 61 cases; 3 of 6 commercial diluents and thickeners essentially pure vitamin E acetate. Screening (Muthumalage et al.): over 500 chemicals in cartridge liquids; no counts per compound.

evidence.locator: Methods › Case Definitions; Table 1 (Case Definitions for Patients with EVALI)
evidence.extracted: CDC case definitions as printed in the paper: confirmed and probable cases both need vaping or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate on chest imaging and no evidence in the medical record of an alternative plausible diagnosis; confirmed cases also need a negative respiratory viral panel, a negative influenza test (if local epidemiology supports influenza testing) and negative results for all other clinically indicated infection tests; probable cases may have an infection identified, or incomplete testing, when the clinical team judges the infection is not the sole cause of the lung injury. State and local health departments assigned case status.

evidence.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Case status row)
evidence.extracted: As of 14 January 2020, all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico had reported 2,668 hospitalized EVALI patients to CDC: 1,401 (53%) confirmed and 1,267 (47%) probable cases.

evidence.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Sex, Median age, Age group, Race/Ethnicity rows)
evidence.extracted: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); 404 (15%) aged 13 to 17, 979 (37%) 18 to 24, 631 (24%) 25 to 34, 335 (13%) 35 to 44, 223 (9%) 45 to 64, 47 (2%) 65 and over, of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 73% non-Hispanic white and 15% Hispanic.

evidence.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Substances used rows and footnotes)
evidence.extracted: Among 2,022 patients with information on substances used (76% of 2,668), who had vaped or dabbed at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset: any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%); any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%); both 834 (41%); THC only 669 (33%); nicotine only 274 (14%); neither 44 (2%). Product information was missing for 24% of patients. The four exclusive categories add to 1,821, not 2,022.

evidence.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title
evidence.extracted: Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI reported to CDC (Figure 1: 2,398 patients by week of admission, February 2019 to 14 January 2020) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and declined steadily after that to the end of the data.

Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system uneven and changing over time. The case counts are of hospitalized patients (the Methods say states report hospitalized or deceased patients); the report does not report deaths or what happened to patients after discharge (it says long-term consequences need long-term follow-up).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to THC-containing products used by EVALI patients (citing the lung-fluid study), that a minority of patients consistently report only nicotine-containing products (possible reasons: patients may not report or know the content of what they vaped; the high sensitivity of the case definition likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have EVALI; or the reports may be accurate), and that evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern, in THC- or non-THC-containing products, in some cases. It is not known whether additives other than vitamin E acetate could cause similar injury.
evidence.quote: evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern

evidence.extracted: Lung-lavage (BAL) fluid from 51 patients with EVALI in 16 states (collected August to December 2019 during routine clinical care; 25 confirmed, 26 probable; median age 23, 69% male) and from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University tobacco-product study (52 who neither vaped nor smoked, 18 who vaped nicotine only, 29 who smoked cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). The authors call the cases a convenience sample; collection was not standardized. New York is not among the 16 states.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (vitamin E acetate row)
evidence.extracted: Vitamin E acetate was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients (94%) and from none of the 99 healthy participants (0 of 52, 0 of 18, 0 of 29). Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals: patients 83.8% to 98.8%; comparators 0% to 3.7%.

Other priority substances in patients' lung fluid: coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39 (the limonene patient had no vitamin E acetate or THC and reported daily flavoured nicotine products); medium-chain triglyceride oil 0 of 49, plant oil 0 of 49, squalane 0 of 38, squalene 0 of 38, pinenes and 3-carene 0 of 39, petroleum distillates 0 of 12. None of these was found in any comparator.

The three patients without detectable vitamin E acetate were all probable cases, with other plausible diagnoses recorded in Table 4, so all 25 confirmed cases were positive (editors' deduction; exact binomial 95% interval for 25 of 25, 86.3% to 100%, editors' calculation).

THC or its metabolites were found in lung fluid from 40 of 47 patients (85%); 9 of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness had THC or metabolites in lung fluid; nicotine or metabolites in 30 of 47 (64%). Self-reported (43 patients): nicotine products only 7 (16%), THC products only 11 (26%), both 22 (51%).
Healthy comparators: none reported vaping THC products; urine THC biomarkers positive in 21 of 82 (26%); nicotine or metabolites in 52% of lung fluids; all negative for every priority substance.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Second-hand context quoted by the authors from CDC and FDA web pages and earlier CDC reports (none read here): more than 2,400 hospitalized patients and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019 (CDC web page); 78% under 35; nearly half (47%) needed intensive care for respiratory failure (earlier CDC report). FDA testing (FDA web page) found vitamin E acetate in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products; in Minnesota (earlier MMWR report) 0 of 10 products seized in 2018 contained it against 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019.

Limits stated by the authors: vitamin E acetate may be a marker of another toxicant; products formed when it is heated were not examined; sample collection was not standardized; timing and burden of exposure could not be assessed; case and comparator samples come from independent studies at single time points, so unknown confounding remains. Animal studies are needed to show whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury.

Funding as printed: National Cancer Institute grant P50CA180908; FDA Center for Tobacco Products grant P30CA016058; Ohio State University Pelotonia Intramural Research. Authors are mostly CDC staff, with Ohio State University and FDA authors; the publisher's disclosure forms were not read.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Thirty-eight samples of fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with EVALI for whom cartridges were obtained; two held nicotine and no cannabinoids and 36 held cannabinoids. The laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019.

evidence.locator: Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (VEA column); Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Vitamin E acetate was found in 23 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%), at 16 to 57% by mass (Table 1 maximum 57.6%; 58% in the Discussion); 13 held none above 1% by mass. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 46% to 79%, treating the 36 fluids as independent, which they are not.

Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil, another diluent, was estimated at 3 to 24% by mass in the 15 fluids the text says held it (Table 1 marks 14, by the editors' count); 12 of the 13 fluids without vitamin E acetate held MCT oil and 2 held both. MCT was estimated roughly because standards for its components are not available.

evidence.locator: Results 3.1, 5th paragraph; Results 3.3; Table 2; Discussion 4.1, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Pesticides: myclobutanil was quantified in 22 fluids (up to 28.3 micrograms per gram), the pesticide synergist piperonyl butoxide in 18 (up to 24.1), and several other fungicides, insecticides and acaricides above 1 microgram per gram in 26; 31 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids held at least one (editors' count). The authors judge the pattern intermittent and say EVALI is not due to a single pesticide. No mycotoxins (below 4.8 ng/g) and no synthetic cannabinoids or opioids (below 0.05% by mass) in any fluid.

Of six commercial products bought online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners, two diluents and one thickener were essentially pure vitamin E acetate; the others were squalane-based or alpha-bisabolol-based. The sellers did not list ingredients on label or website.

Update to 12 December 2019, given in the Conclusions without methods or a table: 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 with THC and 59 with nicotine; 101 of the 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) held vitamin E acetate. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 61% to 76%, treating fluids as independent. Whether the first 38 fluids are included is not stated. The authors also cite CDC counts of 2,409 hospitalized cases and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019, and 205 New York cases including 2 deaths as of 10 December.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.1; Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph; Discussion 4.3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions
evidence.extracted: Limits and inferences stated by the authors: the cause or causes of EVALI are unknown; extensive in vitro and in vivo studies are required to establish a causative role of vitamin E acetate or other agents. The paper has no cartridges from people who vaped without injury, gives no per-patient results, and does not say how the cartridges were judged illicit; its contrast with the laboratory's medical-program products is stated without data.

evidence.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors work at the New York State Department of Health (Wadsworth Center; Center for Environmental Health), the University at Albany and Albany Medical Center.

A library-matched GC-MS screen of liquid from 38 counterfeit or patient-provided THC cartridges, 4 CBD cartridges and medical-grade cartridges found more than 500 chemicals. Chemicals described as specific to the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges include silicon compounds (siloxanes, tetramethyl silicate), esters, benzophenone, glycerol tricaprylate, terpenes and vitamin E acetate; Table 1 lists 47 entries for these cartridges against 13 for CBD and 15 for medical-grade (editors' count). No count of cartridges containing any compound is given.

Aerosol from counterfeit cartridges, collected in one-litre bottles and sent to a commercial laboratory, held over 50 listed volatile compounds (Table 2 has 53 entries), seven of them on the FDA list of tobacco-smoke constituents; silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant elements in the liquid, up to 600 parts per million. Vapor-phase and metals results are shown for counterfeit cartridges only.

The authors say they found vitamin E acetate in many EVALI-associated liquids but not all, and that the other cartridges patients used earlier may have held it; medical-grade cartridges (number not stated; one is described as the reference) held retinol (vitamin A) acetate rather than vitamin E acetate and fewer contaminants than counterfeit cartridges, though some harmful chemicals were still identified in them.

Conclusion as written: numerous respiratory toxicants in liquid and vapor phases were not present in medical or CBD products; a combination of hydrocarbons, oils, other toxic compounds and metals may contribute to EVALI together with vitamin E acetate rather than a single agent. The study is a laboratory screen with library-matched identifications, small comparison groups and no per-cartridge counts; the paper is not a review.

evidence.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors work at the University of Rochester Medical Center, The College at Brockport, the New York State Department of Health Center for Environmental Health and the University at Buffalo.

risk_of_bias.note: All four study cards are rated high overall: the surveillance report has missing and self-reported product data and a sensitive case definition; the lung-fluid comparison used healthy volunteers from another study, sampled mostly before 2019, none of whom vaped THC; the cartridge studies had no comparison cartridges and gave no per-patient results; the screening paper's identifications are library matches without counts.

inconsistency.note: The studies agree in direction. The share holding vitamin E acetate differs (94% of patients' lung fluid; 64% of 36 cartridge fluids, 69% of 147 in a later update; 49% of case-associated THC product samples in FDA testing as quoted second-hand), which different sample types and sources can explain.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and products sampled.

imprecision.note: 48 of 51 and 0 of 99 are precise as counts.

grade.reasoning: Observational: a surveillance case series, a case-comparator lung-fluid study and laboratory analyses of cartridges, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1 (all four study cards rated high overall); the rating cannot fall below very low. Not upgraded for a large effect: the 94% against 0% contrast has no adjusted model, and the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC and were sampled mostly before 2019, so the contrast probably overstates what separates vitamin E acetate from other features of THC cartridge use in 2019. Not downgraded for inconsistency (the studies agree in direction; the proportions differ for reasons of sample type and source), imprecision (the counts are precise) or indirectness (the claim is worded for the people and products sampled). Strict reading: the presence of vitamin E acetate in nearly all lung fluid tested and in most THC-containing cartridge fluids sampled is consistent across two laboratories, but the rating applies to the association and to the description as worded; that it is the cause or the only cause is a separate claim that none of these studies tests, and is lower still. Status replicated: two independent laboratories (CDC with state laboratories; New York State Department of Health), different patients (New York is not among the 16 states of the lung-fluid study) and different sample types, same direction; a third laboratory (University of Rochester) found it in many but not all cartridge liquids, without counts. The earlier CDC report of 29 patients (whether its patients are among the 51 is not stated) and the New York update of 206 fluids (which presumably includes the 38) are not counted as further replications.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only. CDC's recommendation sentences are deliberately not carried. Deaths (52) and intensive care (47%) are second-hand: the CDC update read reports neither; Blount 2020 and Duffy 2020 quote them from a CDC web page and an earlier CDC report. Not read: the earlier MMWR reports and the FDA, Utah and Minnesota product testing cited by the papers (DOIs: Moritz 2019 10.15585/mmwr.mm6843e1; Ellington 2020 10.15585/mmwr.mm6902e2; Chatham-Stephens 2019 10.15585/mmwr.mm6846e1; Taylor 2019 10.15585/mmwr.mm6847e1; Lewis 2019 10.15585/mmwr.mm6842e1; Blount 2019 MMWR 10.15585/mmwr.mm6845e2; Siegel 2019 10.15585/mmwr.mm6841e3). 'Illicit' and 'counterfeit' are the cartridge papers' own labels; Duffy 2020 gives no basis for 'illicit', and Muthumalage 2020 lists brand names recovered from patients and sources (local vape shops, patients) without saying how counterfeit status was established; the CDC update does not report where patients got products. Muthumalage 2020 is a laboratory screening study, not a review as the reading list says. Editors' intervals and deductions need the second reader's recomputation. No awaited PDF is needed for this claim.
